title: Spinner's End
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 8 of 40
content:
Three days later, Snape asked me to go home with him.

He phrased it as an order.

“You will accompany me to Spinner's End tomorrow.”

I looked up from a crate of shrivelfigs. “Will I?”

“Yes.”

“Is this a kidnapping?”

“If it were, I would have chosen someone less conversational.”

His voice had returned, though it remained rough and he rationed it more carefully. Madam Pomfrey had forbidden interviews for a week. Snape had celebrated by speaking only when necessary and using his restored voice primarily for insults.

“What are we retrieving?” I asked.

“Books. Personal ingredients. Several journals relevant to the evidence review.”

“Why do you need me?”

He gave me a look.

I waited.

His jaw tightened.

“Because,” he said at last, “I am not permitted to carry more than fifteen pounds.”

I tried very hard not to smile.

His eyes narrowed.

“I see.”

“You see nothing.”

“Of course.”

“And because the house may have been searched.”

That erased the humor.

“Ministry?”

“Or others.”

“Then we go together.”

“I had already established that.”

The next morning, we traveled by Floo to a public hearth in Cokeworth because the connection at his house had been damaged.

The town was gray even under summer light.

Rows of brick houses pressed against narrow streets. Old mill chimneys rose beyond rooftops like blackened fingers. The river smelled faintly of metal and rain.

Snape wore Muggle clothes beneath a long black coat. Nothing elaborate. Trousers, boots, a white shirt buttoned high enough to cover his scar.

Without robes, he looked less like Professor Snape and more like a man who had forgotten how to live anywhere but inside his own defenses.

He caught me looking.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You should retire that word.”

“You'd miss it.”

“I assure you—”

He stopped.

Across the street, two boys were throwing stones at a rusted sign.

Snape's face had gone distant.

“Did you grow up here?” I asked.

The question was relevant enough to the trip that I risked it.

“Yes.”

“Do you want me to stop asking questions?”

“Yes.”

“Fine.”

He looked almost suspicious of my compliance.

Spinner's End was narrower than I expected. The houses crowded close together, soot-darkened and tired. Snape's stood near the end of the row with curtains drawn and paint peeling around the door.

He stopped at the gate.

For a moment, he did nothing.

I understood that threshold better than I wanted to.

A place could be yours and still require courage to enter.

“You can wait outside,” he said.

“I thought I was here to carry things.”

“You are.”

“Then I'll need access to the things.”

His mouth tightened.

He opened the gate.

The front door had been forced.

Snape's wand was in his hand immediately.

Mine followed.

“Behind me,” he said.

“No.”

His head snapped toward me.

“Beside you.”

“This is not the time—”

“Exactly.”

He looked furious.

Then he shifted half a step, making room.

We entered together.

The house smelled of dust, old paper, and damp brick.

The sitting room had been searched. Drawers pulled out. Cushions cut open. Books scattered across the floor. A framed photograph lay face down near the hearth.

Snape did not pick it up.

He moved through the room methodically, checking corners and doors.

No one remained.

The kitchen was worse.

Cabinets stood open. A jar of dried nettles had smashed across the tile. Someone had carved TRAITOR into the wooden table.

Snape stared at the word.

His face went completely blank.

I hated whoever had written it.

Not because the word was entirely false.

That was the cruel part.

He had betrayed people. More than once. He had betrayed Lily's trust as a boy. He had betrayed the Order when he joined Voldemort. He had betrayed Voldemort when he turned spy. He had deceived colleagues, students, enemies, allies.

The insult had been chosen because it could attach itself to truth.

I raised my wand.

The carved letters vanished beneath a repair charm.

Snape looked at me.

“I did not ask you to do that.”

“I know.”

“You should not alter potential evidence.”

“I photographed it first.”

I held up the small enchanted plate from my case.

His eyes dropped to it.

Then back to the clean table.

“Efficient,” he said.

It sounded like thank you.

Upstairs, his bedroom had been disturbed but not destroyed. A narrow bed stood against the wall. Shelves bowed beneath books. A desk faced a small window overlooking the backs of neighboring houses.

There was almost nothing decorative.

No trophies. No framed certificates. No evidence of twenty years at Hogwarts beyond a black teaching robe hanging behind the door.

On the desk sat a photograph of a thin, dark-haired woman with heavy brows.

Snape crossed the room and turned it face down.

“My mother,” he said before I could look away.

I nodded.

He opened a cupboard.

Inside were jars of ingredients organized with absolute precision.

I smiled.

“What?”

“Alphabetical.”

He froze.

I pointed.

“Asphodel. Belladonna. Chizpurfle carapace. Dittany.”

His face became offended.

“This is a domestic cupboard.”

“So alphabetization is morally acceptable at home.”

“It is space-efficient here.”

“I will be noting this in the audit.”

“You will do no such thing.”

The tension eased by a fraction.

We packed journals into two cases. Some were school-era notes. Others documented brewing under Voldemort's orders, encoded in a system only Snape understood.

“Why keep them?” I asked.

He paused.

“Because destroying records does not destroy acts.”

That answer stayed with me.

In the back room, we found the personal ingredients he wanted: rare resins, preserved venom sacs, powdered stone, a sealed tin of something that hissed when moved.

“What is that?” I asked.

“Nothing you need.”

“It hisses.”

“So do I, on occasion.”

“I've noticed.”

By late afternoon, the cases were full.

Snape sat on the edge of the bed while I sealed them. He looked exhausted.

“Five minutes,” I said.

“I did not ask.”

“Neither did your nervous system.”

He was too tired to argue properly.

I sat on the desk chair.

For a while we listened to the street outside.

A lorry passed.

Someone shouted from a garden.

A radio played through an open window two houses away.

“This is where you learned about magic?” I asked.

He looked at the floor.

“I already knew of it. My mother was a witch.”

“And your father?”

“A Muggle.”

The word contained no contempt. Only weariness.

“Did he know?”

“Yes.”

“Did he like it?”

A humorless smile.

“My father liked very little.”

I knew better than to ask more.

Snape's eyes moved to the window.

“I used to watch for her from here.”

I went still.

He did not say Lily's name.

He did not need to.

“She lived nearby?”

“Close enough.”

His voice had gone rough again, but this time I suspected the scar was not responsible.

“I thought Hogwarts would solve everything,” he said.

The admission was so quiet I almost missed it.

“Did it?”

He gave me a sidelong look.

“Clearly.”

I smiled despite myself.

Then he added, “It gave me different problems.”

“That tends to be what escape does.”

His gaze sharpened.

I wondered if I had revealed too much.

He did not ask.

I appreciated that.

When the five minutes became ten, he stood.

We carried the cases downstairs together, though I took the heavier one before he could protest.

At the front door, he looked back into the house.

“Are you keeping it?” I asked.

“I have not decided.”

“It doesn't seem to like you much.”

“Houses do not have opinions.”

“This one feels judgmental.”

“It has had poor examples.”

We stepped outside.

Snape locked the door with three spells.

As we walked toward the public Floo, rain began to fall.

He did not hurry.

Neither did I.

For the first time since meeting him, I had seen the place where Severus Snape had begun.

It did not explain him.

Nothing could excuse every choice made by the adult because of pain suffered by the child.

But the gray streets, the narrow room, the turned-down photograph, the books stacked like escape routes—all of it added context where gossip had only supplied judgment.

At the corner, Snape glanced at me.

“You are quiet.”

“I can be.”

“Rarely.”

“Do you want me to say something?”

He considered.

“No.”

So I walked beside him in the rain.

This time, silence did not feel like distance.
